source.title: Can sparse autoencoders make sense of gene expression latent variable models?

record.tranche_reason: The study measures recovery of simulated ground-truth variables from latent representations and SAE features, and finds that recovery depends on where variables occur in the generative process; it also reports no significant SAE advantage over simple baselines for recovering known variables. This refines the scope of claims about superposition and feature recovery, although it does not directly test the geometric arrangement of directions.
record.gate_note: The paper’s introductory statements about superposition and its citations to other studies are not results. Hyperparameters and values used only to select settings are not rows. The simulation results in Supplementary Table 5 report feature-variable correlations and are recorded below; the paper’s claims about recovery patterns are described in the verdict and authors’ conclusion.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool and benchmarks how well they recover simulated gene-expression generative variables, then applies them to single-cell models. Its 'superposition' is linear-regression recoverability of variables from autoencoder latents. It has no sparse-features-exceed-dimensions toy setup, no geometry, no capacity or polysemanticity test, and no LLMs. The SAE-versus-ground-truth results concern recovery of data-generating variables, not whether SAE features are the model's own canonical units. So no version is tested; the relevant findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the following points. SAEs recovered hidden variables well when those variables were learned in superposition, and recovery improved with SAE hidden dimensionality and model width. Variables with indirect effect and little structure could practically not be recovered. SAE-feature/observable connectivity recovered 75–95% of generative structure. In single-cell models, SAE features were biologically meaningful and could steer cells.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses biological-style simulated generative data and measures regression-based recovery of variables and SAE-feature correlations, rather than the original toy-model analysis of sparse-feature geometric configurations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported recovery varies with a variable’s position in the generative process; the paper also reports effects associated with variable type/distribution and AE depth, width, and latent dimension. In the SAE sweep, outcomes depend on architecture and hyperparameters including hidden dimension, L1 weight or k, and learning rate.

fits_no_version.finding: On large simulated data (AE latent 150), SAE features recover X'' (0.74) about as well as PCA (0.72). They do worse than ICA on X (0.19 vs 0.50). The author reports no significant SAE advantage over PCA/ICA/SVD baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs offer no advantage over linear baselines for recovering known ground-truth generative variables from latent embeddings.

fits_no_version.finding: Recoverability of hidden variables from AE latents (regression R2) depends on their position in the generative process: X'' best, then A, B, X', X. Distant variables are recovered worse in larger models despite lower loss (Fig 1C, S2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which data-generating variables a network represents linearly depends on their causal distance from the observables and on their distribution type.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on multiDGD and Geneformer embeddings of the same bone-marrow data share all 2499 GO terms. Feature-level optimal bipartite matching similarity is only 0.16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features from different models trained on the same data share broad semantics but differ at the individual-feature level.

record.problems: The study does not directly measure feature angles or near-orthogonality, and the simulation’s variable-recovery measure is not a direct test of superposition geometry. Table S5 reports an average over 4 SAE scaling factors rather than individual runs.

untested.parts: Near-orthogonal overlapping directions, sparsity-dependent phase transition and regular geometry are not examined. The simulated data are not the toy sparse-feature setup.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable and canonical units of a model's representation is not directly tested. Seed robustness covers only counts of live/local/global neurons (Table S6).

record.verdict_notes: Uses 'superposition' loosely to mean linear recoverability of variables from latents. Biological domain (simulated counts, multiDGD, Geneformer), not LLMs. The record's V1 'tested' status and limits_scope label are dropped: no row measures what V1 names.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not directly test near-orthogonality, overlap geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric configurations. Its simulated data and recovery measures differ from the original toy-model setup.
Capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, and polysemanticity are not tested.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure are not tested.
The pretrained models are biological single-cell models, not LLMs; the study does not test feature distribution across LLM neurons or SAE recovery in LLMs.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete or canonical units, nor their stability as individual units. The cross-model comparison concerns GO annotations and feature-space similarity.
The dimensionality of features as directions versus multidimensional features is not tested.

relation.reason: Uses superposition and SAEs to interpret biological embeddings, reporting method performance without directly testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Sections 4–5 benchmark SAE variable recovery and biological interpretation. Regression recoverability does not test the specified toy geometry, capacity explanation, LLM representations, dictionary canonicality, or feature dimensionality.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v3 dated 29 July 2025. Table S5 reports signed correlations; SAE uncertainties are SEM across four hidden scaling factors. The large simulation has 100 X variables and 20,000 observables.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: large simulated data, AE latent dimension 150
reader_labels.reason: Individual SAE-feature recovery is uneven across generative variables, and original X is not directly represented by individual SAE features (rows S5-SAE-Xpp, S5-SAE-Xp, S5-SAE-X, S5-SAE-A, S5-SAE-B). This qualifies recoverability in this setting, but does not decide the proposed geometry.
